8.1.l: Pediatric Hip — Late Sequelae of the Septic Hip
8.1.b:
A septic hip treated late leaves a hip that grows wrong for years; this chapter is that damaged hip.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what are the sequelae of a septic hip?"
- "Head and neck **destruction**, physeal arrest and **pathological dislocation**."
- "Then **leg-length discrepancy**, coxa vara or valga, stiffness and early arthritis."
- "First question in every film: is the hip **stable**?"

### Definition
Sequelae are what remains once the infection is gone.
[[FIG: Fig 8.1 · 8.1
- **Late sequelae**: residual deformity of the hip after acute septic arthritis
- Acute septic hip and its drainage → 07 Septic Arthritis
- The infection may damage cartilage, epiphysis, physis, neck and acetabulum together
- The vulnerable epiphyseal blood supply lets the damage come fast

### Who Gets Them
The worst hips belong to the youngest, latest-treated infants.
- Severe sequelae follow infection in **infancy**, mostly the neonatal period
- Choi's poor prognostic factors: young infant, **prematurity**, symptoms **>4 days** (Campbell)
- The most crucial factor is **delay in diagnosis**

| Delay before drainage | Unsatisfactory radiological result (Lee 2015) |
|---|---|
| ≈2.5 days | 25% |
| ≈4.7 days | **50%** |
| ≈6.9 days | 75% |

MEMORY HOOK — the four-day clock
- Every day of pus in a baby's hip is a day off the femoral head's life; at four days, half the hips are already lost.

8.2.l: Pediatric Hip — Late Sequelae of the Septic Hip
8.2.b:
Pus and pressure hit several growing parts at once, so the shapes are endless.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what does the infection damage?"
- "**Cartilage** necrosis, epiphyseal **AVN** and **physeal** arrest."
- "Neck destruction or **pseudarthrosis**, and loss of the head."
- "A **dislocated** hip, a dysplastic acetabulum and a short limb."

### Sites of Damage
Each tissue hit gives its own late deformity.

| Tissue hit | Late result |
|---|---|
| Articular cartilage | cartilage necrosis → stiffness, ankylosis |
| Epiphysis | **AVN** (avascular necrosis), deformed head, coxa magna |
| Physis | arrest → short neck, **coxa vara or valga**, LLD (leg-length discrepancy) |
| Neck | malalignment or **pseudarthrosis** |
| Head and neck | complete loss, proximal migration |
| Capsule | distension → **pathological dislocation** |
| Acetabulum | dysplasia from an empty or unloaded socket |

- Infection may spread to other bones in the same child
[[FIG: Fig 8.2 · 8.2
- Coxa vara as a deformity in its own right → 10 Coxa Vara

### Four Sources of Disability
Campbell sorts every septic hip complaint into four groups.
- **Pain**: incongruous surfaces or pathological dislocation
- **Stiffness**: partial or complete ankylosis, worse with contracture
- **Deformity**: coxa vara, shortening, flexion–adduction
- **Instability**: bone loss in the proximal femur or dislocation

### The Ossific Nucleus Is Not the Epiphysis
A head that is not seen may still be there.
- The whole infant epiphysis is cartilage; the film shows only the **ossific nucleus** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
[[FIG: Fig 8.3 · 8.2
- MRI may show a good cartilaginous head, neck and joint
[[FIG: Fig 8.4 · 8.2
- So "no head on the film" is not "no head"
[[FIG: Fig 8.5 · 8.2
- Early films can look destroyed and later show **reconstitution**

PITFALL — the headless film
- Calling a hip headless because the ossific nucleus is missing leads to needless surgery
- Say → "**the cartilage head may be present; I judge by stability and follow up**"

8.3.l: Pediatric Hip — Late Sequelae of the Septic Hip
8.3.b:
Several schemes exist because the shapes are many; two questions matter: stable, and is there a head?

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you classify septic sequelae?"
- "**Choi** (1990): four types, I to IV, by head–neck damage; the most used."
- "**Hunka** (1982): types 1 to 5, by the epiphysis and stability."
- "**Forlin** (2008): stable or dislocated, head present or absent."

| Scheme | Year | Based on |
|---|---|---|
| **Hunka** | 1982 | capital epiphysis present or not, hip stability |
| **Choi** | 1990 | radiographic damage of head, physis and neck |
| **Forlin** | 2008 | reduced or dislocated, head present or absent |

### Hunka Classification
The first scheme counts what is left of the head and whether it holds.
[[FIG: Fig 8.6 · 8.3

| Type | Picture (Hunka, as given by Pafilas) |
|---|---|
| **1** | minimal or no head change |
| **2A** | head deformed, physis open |
| **2B** | head deformed, physis closed |
| **3** | femoral neck **pseudarthrosis** |
| **4A** | head destroyed, **stable** neck segment |
| **4B** | head destroyed, **unstable** neck segment |
| **5** | head and neck destroyed, hip **dislocated** |

- Types 4 and 5 behave as pseudarthroses: the femur migrates up on loading
- They are the classic indication for a **pelvic support osteotomy**

### Choi Classification
Choi's four types climb from a scarred head to a missing proximal femur.

| Type | Damage (Choi 1990) | What it needs |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | transient epiphyseal ischaemia; IA none, IB mild coxa magna | no reconstruction |
| **II** | deformed epiphysis, physis and metaphysis | prevent subluxation |
| **III** | neck malalignment (IIIA) or neck pseudarthrosis (IIIB) | realignment osteotomy or bone graft |
| **IV** | head and neck destroyed; IVA medial neck remnant, IVB none | stabilize, equalize length |

#### Type II Details
- Coxa magna with a deformed head, or premature physeal closure with a **short neck**
- Aims: acetabular cover, abductor efficiency, equal limb length

#### Type III
- Extreme anteversion or retroversion, or a neck **pseudarthrosis**
[[FIG: Fig 8.7 · 8.3
- Early proximal femoral realignment or grafting of the pseudarthrosis (Choi 2005)

#### Type IVA
- Only a small medial remnant of the neck base remains
[[FIG: Fig 8.8 · 8.3

#### Type IVB
- Head and neck are gone; the hip is high and unstable
[[FIG: Fig 8.9 · 8.3

- The prevalence in Choi's series: I 15%, II 32%, III 15%, IV **38%**
- Weakness: hard to apply in infants, poor agreement (7 of 41 hips concordant)

### Forlin Classification
The lecturer's choice, because it predicts treatment (Prof Abdel-Ghani).

| Group | Hip | Head |
|---|---|---|
| **1A** | stable, reduced | present |
| **1B** | stable, reduced | absent |
| **2A** | unstable, dislocated | present |
| **2B** | unstable, dislocated | absent |
[[FIG: Fig 8.10–8.13 · 8.3

- Agreement was better than Choi's: 25 of 41 hips (Forlin)
- Objection: a "visible head" changes with age, as the nucleus ossifies late
- A 2025 two-type modification (HHPO) uses the same two questions
[[FIG: Fig 8.14 · 8.3

MEMORY HOOK — two doors
- Forlin is a house with two doors: is the hip inside (stable)? is anybody home (head)? Four rooms, four plans.

8.4.l: Pediatric Hip — Late Sequelae of the Septic Hip
8.4.b:
The child walks in limping and short, often with a painless hip that once hurt badly.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how does a septic sequela present?"
- "A limp, **shortening** and a positive Trendelenburg sign."
- "A history of **neonatal sepsis**, an incubator, or a red swollen hip."
- "A dislocated hip that **once hurt**: septic, not DDH."

### History
Ask the family the questions that DDH never needs.
- Admission to an **incubator** or NICU (neonatal intensive care unit)
- Crying when the mother changed the nappy
- An abscess, or redness over the hip
- Previous drainage, osteomyelitis, other joints infected

### Septic Dislocation Versus DDH
At first glance a septic dislocation looks like DDH (developmental dysplasia of the hip).

| Feature | DDH | Septic sequela |
|---|---|---|
| Pain in history | **never** | yes |
| Capsule at surgery | lax | adherent, fibrotic |
| Acetabulum | shallow, full of pulvinar | may be filled by fibrous tissue |
| Prognosis after reduction | DDH figures | worse, not the same |

- Types of hip dislocation: traumatic, **septic**, paralytic, developmental (Nagah)

PITFALL — the painful DDH
- A dislocated hip with a history of pain is not DDH
- Say → "**DDH is painless; a painful dislocation in infancy is septic until proved otherwise**"

### Examination
The examination answers the stability question the film may not.
- **Gait**: Trendelenburg lurch, short-limb gait
- **Telescoping** test: push and pull the femur; movement means instability
- Causes of telescoping: DDH, septic hip, paralytic dislocation, femoral neck nonunion
- Range of motion, fixed adduction or abduction, LLD by blocks
- Abductor power: a high trochanter weakens it

8.5.l: Pediatric Hip — Late Sequelae of the Septic Hip
8.5.b:
The plain film decides most things; extra tests only answer a planning question.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you assess the hip on a film?"
- "**Shenton line** intact and a sclerotic **sourcil** = stable hip."
- "A white sourcil with no head seen means a loaded cartilage head."
- "Long-leg films for LLD; MRI or arthrogram only if it changes the plan."

### Signs of a Stable Hip
Two signs say the femur is bearing weight in the socket.

| Sign | Stable hip | Unstable hip |
|---|---|---|
| **Shenton line** | intact | broken |
| **Sourcil** (radiological roof) | white, sclerotic | not white |
| Standing | stays in | rides up |
| Telescoping | negative | positive |

- A loaded cartilage head concentrates load on the roof → white **sclerotic sourcil**
- Head unseen but sourcil white → the black "empty" area is **cartilage**
- No sourcil and no head or neck → test telescoping
[[FIG: Fig 8.15 · 8.5

### Instability
Instability is more than a dislocated film.
- Dislocated, dislocatable or subluxatable hips are all unstable
- So is a hip that rides out when the child stands on it

### Other Imaging
Use each test for a defined question.
- **MRI**: cartilage head, neck and joint before planning
- **Arthrogram**: outlines the cartilage head and socket under anaesthesia (Qi 2025)
- **Standing long-leg film or scanogram**: LLD and its level
[[FIG: Fig 8.16 · 8.5
- **CT**: bone stock, version and canal size before arthroplasty
[[FIG: Fig 8.17 · 8.5
- **Maximum adduction** and single-leg standing films: plan a pelvic support osteotomy
- A child walking well with no pain needs no MRI

8.6.l: Pediatric Hip — Late Sequelae of the Septic Hip
8.6.b:
Treat the child, not the film, and decide by stability first.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "what are your treatment principles?"
- "**Wait**: delay reconstruction until the infection is long quiet."
- "**Stable** hip → follow up; **unstable** hip → reduce whatever is left."
- "Address **LLD**; an arthritic hip gets a THR (total hip replacement)."

### Why Wait
Reconstruction is delayed for months or years after the infection (Campbell).
- The risk of reactivating infection falls
- Early films may show reconstitution of the "destroyed" head
- Bone strength improves as necrotic bone revascularizes
- Yet an unstable hip should not go untreated through growth

### Treat the Patient, Not the X-ray
The lecturer's strongest rule is to never operate on expectations.
- A walking child of 1–1.5 years with no pain is followed, even with dysplasia
[[FIG: Fig 8.18 · 8.6
- Judge by the **head**, as in Perthes, not by the acetabular index
- A good head → the acetabulum is not expected to stay dysplastic
- Success is not a nicer X-ray; nobody can predict the adult hip
- Untreated patients often functioned better than operated ones (Betz 1990)

### Activity, Not Casts
Muscles hold this hip in.
- Limiting activity at 1–1.5 years is impossible: do not try
- A cast weakens the **dynamic stabilizers** keeping the head in place
- A moving, playing child improves faster

MEMORY HOOK — the impatient surgeon
- The septic hip rewards the surgeon who drinks his tea slowly: the film at two years is not the hip at twenty.

### Management Algorithm
One question opens the algorithm: is the hip stable?
[[FIG: Fig 8.19 · 8.6

| Hip | Anatomy | Management |
|---|---|---|
| **Stable** | head visible or not | follow up; later correct mechanics |
| **Unstable** | any head or neck left | **open reduction** of the remnant |
| **Unstable** | no head or neck, 2–3 years | **Harmon** osteotomy |
| **Unstable** | no head or neck, older | **pelvic support osteotomy** or **THR** later |
| **All** | shortening | address LLD |
| **Arthritic** | any | THR; no place for reconstruction |

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "stable septic hip, what do you do?"
- "Walking well, no Trendelenburg → **nothing**."
- "Weak abductors → **trochanteric transfer**; no abduction → valgus osteotomy."
- "**Valgus** needs real adduction to take up."

### Observation
Even a hip with no head or neck may stay stable.
[[FIG: Fig 8.20 · 8.7
- A neck alone can make a stable joint
[[FIG: Fig 8.21 · 8.7
- No head and no neck but stable, judged by the sourcil → do nothing
- Harmon is **not** indicated in a stable hip: it may destabilize the femur
[[FIG: Fig 8.22 · 8.7
- The untouched hip was later "nice"; it might have been nicer left alone

### Abductor Insufficiency
Correct mechanics only when the gait shows it is needed.
[[FIG: Fig 8.23 · 8.7

| Problem | Operation |
|---|---|
| Weak abductors, high trochanter | **greater trochanter transfer** |
| Lack of abduction range | **valgus osteotomy** |

- Valgus osteotomy needs **real adduction** to take up (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Valgus without adduction → fixed **abduction** deformity
- An adduction deformity walks better than an abduction deformity

#### Timing of Trochanteric Transfer
- Early transfer stops **greater trochanter growth**
[[FIG: Fig 8.24 · 8.7
- So the transfer waits for the right age

### Neck Lesion With a Good Head
A neck lesion with a preserved head needs only an osteotomy.
[[FIG: Fig 8.25 · 8.7
- Realign by osteotomy; hold the head with **smooth K-wires** only, no screws
[[FIG: Fig 8.26 · 8.7
- Later procedures stay possible
[[FIG: Fig 8.27 · 8.7

### Ankylosis and Fixed Deformity
A stiff hip in bad position is corrected by osteotomy, not by moving it.
- Flexion–adduction ankylosis → intertrochanteric osteotomy (Campbell)
[[FIG: Fig 8.28 · 8.7
- Child: neutral rotation, 0° flexion, **20–30° abduction**
- Adult: **25° flexion**, neutral abduction
- Deformity may recur before maturity: warn of a second osteotomy

The pelvic support osteotomy stops the pelvis dropping by using up all adduction.
[[FIG: Fig 8.45 · 8.8

Campbell lists five ways to stabilize the hip after sepsis.

MUST-KNOW — 60-second answer: "how do you manage the LLD?"
- "Predict the final LLD by the **multiplier** method."
- "Small: shoe raise; 2–5 cm: contralateral **epiphysiodesis**."
- "Large: **lengthening** near maturity, fewest stages."

### Timing and Choice
Length operations come after all hip reconstruction (Campbell).

| Final discrepancy | Treatment |
|---|---|
| ≤1.5 cm | none, or a lift |
| 2–5 cm | contralateral **epiphysiodesis** |
| >5–6 cm | **lengthening** |

- The lecturer lengthens once the expected gap reaches **6 cm** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Never lengthen at 4 cm: it returns, and a second stage follows
- Aim for the **fewest** lengthenings, about 6 cm per session
- At 7 years he waits: neither epiphysiodesis nor lengthening yet
- Measure for 1–3 years, then predict by the **multiplier** app

### Where to Lengthen
The bone segment chosen must have stable joints above and below.
- Osteotomy distal, in the **metaphysis**: room for fixation above and below
- After Harmon, 7 cm short: **tibial lengthening** chosen
[[FIG: Fig 8.59–8.60 · 8.9
- Shortening the long side was no option: femur ≤5–6 cm
- Knees then sit at different levels: cosmetic, not functional

#### Conditions for Femoral Lengthening
- Acetabular index **<20°** and centre-edge angle **>20°** (Prof Abdel-Ghani)
- Good, non-paralytic abductors
- Then the hip will not sublux during distraction

### Osteomyelitis of the Whole Femur
A child's infected femur can rebuild itself if you wait.
[[FIG: Fig 8.61 · 8.9
- Girl with huge thigh swelling: the sequestrum was the whole femur
- Removing it would leave no femur; resection was avoided
- One to two years later the acetabulum, head and neck reappeared
[[FIG: Fig 8.62–8.63 · 8.9
- Children are treated differently from adults
[[FIG: Fig 8.64 · 8.9
- The rest was femoral lengthening without subluxation
[[FIG: Fig 8.65 · 8.9
- Even chronic cases: keep stability, do not rush sequestrectomy
